creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal processing
Correlation
Cross-correlation
Matched filter
Signal detection
dublinCore.description: Copies of a known template are hidden in white Gaussian noise at unknown delays. Cross-correlating the received signal with the template produces a peak at each delay. The MicroSim shows the template, its time-reversed matched filter, the correlation output with threshold detection and per-peak SNR, and a moving-average filter for comparison.

topic: Cross-correlation and matched filtering for detection in noise
Peak SNR gain of the matched filter
Detection threshold, false alarms and missed detections
learningObjectives: Explain how cross-correlation locates a known pattern inside a longer signal
Relate the matched filter to the time-reversed template and to cross-correlation
Calculate the expected peak SNR from the input SNR and the template length
Analyze how input SNR, template length and threshold affect missed detections and false alarms
Compare templates by the sharpness of their correlation peaks and the resulting timing accuracy

misconceptions.misconception: Any smoothing filter detects a signal as well as a matched filter
misconceptions.correction: A filter must be matched to the template shape; a moving average equals the matched filter only for a rectangular pulse
misconceptions.evidence: Tick Moving average: the averager peak is 0.11 for the sine burst, 0.16 for the chirp and 0.38 for the Barker code, against 1.00 for the matched filter, and the two curves coincide only for the rectangular pulse

misconceptions.misconception: A signal below the noise level cannot be detected
misconceptions.correction: The matched filter concentrates the template energy into one sample, giving a peak SNR that is 10 log10(L) dB above the input SNR
misconceptions.evidence: At an input SNR of -3 dB the received trace shows no obvious pattern, yet with the threshold at 0.70 about 93.5% of the signals are found with almost no false alarms

misconceptions.misconception: The matched filter output looks like the template
misconceptions.correction: The output is the correlation of the received signal with the template, which for a noise-free template is its autocorrelation, so a long chirp becomes a narrow spike
misconceptions.evidence: Select the chirp: the template wiggles across 48 samples but the correlation is a single narrow peak

optimizations: The signal model is rebuilt only when a control changes

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Three rows of plots: a noisy received signal containing hidden copies of a template, the template beside its time-reversed matched filter, and the cross-correlation output with a threshold line and detected peaks labelled with their lag and signal-to-noise ratio. Controls choose the template, input SNR, number of signals and threshold, draw new noise, overlay a moving average and show or hide the true delays.

responsiveBreakpoints.description: Below 600 px wider captions are shortened, fonts shrink, option names are abbreviated and the two checkboxes stack

controls.label: Template
controls.description: Chooses the known signal s[n] that is hidden in the noise and used as the correlation template

controls.label: New Noise
controls.description: Draws a new noise record and new random delays

controls.label: Input SNR (dB)
controls.description: Sets the average template power divided by the noise variance, in decibels

controls.label: Number of signals
controls.description: Sets how many copies of the template are hidden in the record

controls.label: Threshold
controls.description: Sets the level the normalized correlation must exceed for a peak to be reported

controls.label: Moving average
controls.description: Overlays the output of an L-sample moving average scaled to the same output noise level

controls.label: True delays
controls.description: Shows the real delays as green bands and dashed lines and scores the detections; unticked, it hides the answers

visualElements.description: Received signal r[n] over 600 samples with optional green bands at the true delays
Stem plots of the template s[n] (blue) and the matched filter h[n] = s[L-1-n] (red)

Normalized cross-correlation in purple with a dashed threshold line, detected peaks labelled with lag and measured SNR, an optional orange dashed moving average and a grey strip for lags without full overlap
Summary box with the expected peak SNR and the number of signals found, false alarms and largest timing error

model.description: Copies of a template are added at random delays to seeded white Gaussian noise. The normalized cross-correlation is thresholded and peaks within a quarter of the template length of a true delay count as detections.
equations: peak SNR = E_s / sigma^2 = L x input SNR
algorithms: Seeded Mulberry32 pseudo-random generator and Box-Muller Gaussian noise
Direct O(N L) cross-correlation and convolution
Local-maximum peak detection with one peak per template length
assumptions: Noise is white and Gaussian, generated by a seeded pseudo-random generator
Input SNR is the average template power divided by the noise variance
Templates are real-valued, so no complex conjugate is needed in the matched filter
A detection within a quarter of the template length of a true delay counts as a hit
limitations: Only lags where the whole template lies inside the 600-sample record are computed
Copies of the template never overlap (at least 1.5 template lengths apart)

instructionalStrategies: Predict the peak SNR from the template length, then compare with the measured value on each peak
Tally missed signals and false alarms over ten noise records at several thresholds
Compare the matched filter with a moving average for each template
extensions: Add a second, different template and detect both from one record
Replace the white noise by coloured noise and discuss the whitening filter
